blocks.html: Today’s long read: The machine that weighed the gold - how Titan went from JRD Tata’s watch bet in 1984 to a near-death jewellery business in the late 1990s, and how an X-ray machine that proved India’s jewellers were short-changing their customers became the foundation of the country’s largest jewellery brand. Read it here.
The sweep: FIIs bought a net Rs 14,975 crore on Thursday - the most in over a year - while domestic funds sold Rs 10,445 crore; the Sensex gained 2,008.61 points (2.60%) to 79,310.01, banks in front.
The overnight rout: the Nasdaq fell 5.5% into correction and the S&P 500 lost 4.4% - the worst session since April 2025 - on data-center political risk; the Magnificent Seven shed $1 trillion.
Oil’s U-turn: Brent settled up more than $3 after Iran’s navy said a tanker struck a mine and caught fire east of Hormuz - one day after both benchmarks crashed 8%.

The prints and the verdicts: Titan’s profit more than doubled to Rs 2,393 crore (a one-off helped) and ONGC’s rose 47% with an Rs 8 dividend - both reported after the close, so their verdicts land today; Thursday’s actual verdicts: Lenskart hit a 52-week high, Nykaa fell, PI Industries fell 18.9% on a 70% profit drop.
The exchange’s verdict: BSE Ltd jumped 5% after its 45% quarter; Motilal Oswal kept its Buy, Bernstein stayed Underperform at a higher target.
The long read: Titan - the watch company saved by a purity machine. Read it.

1. The biggest foreign buying day in over a year. Foreign institutional investors bought a net Rs 14,974.68 crore of Indian equities on Thursday - the largest single-day purchase in more than a year, surpassing the previous record of Rs 12,594 crore set on 26 June 2025, on gross purchases of Rs 31,797.86 crore against sales of Rs 16,823.18 crore (Moneycontrol, on exchange data). The other side of the trade is just as striking: domestic institutions sold a net Rs 10,444.54 crore. The market roared: the Sensex jumped 2,008.61 points (2.60%) to 79,310.01 and the Nifty 576 points (2.40%) to 24,536.60, with Bajaj Finance up 7.77% - the top Sensex gainer - and ICICI Bank up 5.29% (India Today’s wrap; stock prices are BSE official closes). Financial services led every sector table. The buying is a sharp reversal from the foreign outflows that ran through most of 2026, and it lands on the eve of a Diwali weekend - Diwali falls on Sunday this year (News18). Editor’s takeaway: one record session does not make a trend - the test of this reversal is whether the buying survives what New York did a few hours later (story 2).

2. Wall Street’s AI trade broke overnight. After Indian markets closed, the Nasdaq composite plunged 5.5% to 24,315 - entering a correction, more than 10% below its 6 October high of 27,599.79 - the S&P 500 fell 4.4% to 7,353, and the Dow dropped 1,833 points (3.4%) to 51,523, all the worst single-day performances since the April 2025 tariff selloff (Kiplinger’s closing report). The Magnificent Seven lost about $1 trillion of market value in the session; Nvidia slumped 9.3% and turned negative for the year, with Meta down 4.0% and Microsoft down 3.6% (CNBC). All eleven S&P sectors closed lower. The stated catalyst, per Kiplinger: concern that Democratic leadership in Washington and in states “from Texas to Ohio” will create headwinds for the AI data-center buildout - the political-licence risk this paper flagged on Monday and priced on Wednesday, now repriced violently in one session. Qualcomm added an earnings wound, sinking 9.5% on a weak outlook. Editor’s takeaway: the correction is in the AI trade’s foundation stocks, not its fringe - what to watch is whether Thursday’s sellers treat this as a valuation reset or the start of a capex reappraisal; Monday’s Mumbai open inherits the gap either way.

3. Oil’s 8% crash lasted one day. Brent settled up more than $3 a barrel on Thursday and WTI up more than $2, reversing part of Wednesday’s collapse to two-month lows, after fresh attacks on tankers fed supply worries (Reuters). Iran’s navy said an oil tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz struck a mine and caught fire, and accused the ship of breaching regulations by operating in an “unsafe zone” (The National). The diplomacy continues in parallel: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held calls with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts on de-escalation, per Tasnim. Wednesday’s crash, recall, was the market pricing Tuesday’s election as de-escalation; Thursday’s attack is the counter-evidence arriving within 24 hours. Eurasia Group’s base case: any escalation in the conflict could push Brent into a $110 to $125 range. Editor’s takeaway: the war premium came out in one session and started going back in within one session - the detained tankers and the seven-conditions reply chain remain the tripwires.

4. The results flood: the prints, and the verdicts that already landed. Thursday evening brought the heavyweight prints - all after the close, so their market verdicts land today, Friday. Titan: consolidated profit more than doubled, up 114% to Rs 2,393 crore - though the jump partly reflects a one-off gain from the change in gold customs duty; adjusted pre-tax profit grew 18%, and revenue of Rs 20,614 crore missed street estimates of Rs 22,453 crore (Hindu BusinessLine; Mint). ONGC: consolidated profit up 47% to Rs 18,535 crore with an Rs 8 interim dividend; standalone profit of Rs 15,489 crore missed the poll estimate of Rs 15,591 crore (CNBC TV18). M&M: standalone profit of Rs 5,102 crore beat the Rs 4,757 crore poll, on revenue up 27% to Rs 42,477 crore. Thursday’s actual verdicts were on Wednesday’s prints, and the two gaps resolved in opposite directions: Lenskart (profit up 122.1% to Rs 227.08 crore, revenue up 35.7% to Rs 2,845 crore) hit a 52-week high of 767.40 intraday before closing up 3.96% at 718.40, with a wall of upgrades - Nomura, Jefferies, Elara, HSBC, Motilal Oswal, CLSA and Macquarie raising targets, and Citi the lone Neutral (Economic Times; Hindu BusinessLine); Nykaa’s 200%-plus profit jump to about Rs 101 crore failed to impress the street, and the stock closed down 1.44% at 350.00 (Business Standard). The day’s cautionary print: PI Industries - profit down 70% to Rs 122 crore on weak agri exports and margin contraction, the stock down 18.86% to Rs 1,774.30, a six-year low per Business Standard (CNBC TV18). Editor’s takeaway: the flood is rewarding beats and punishing misses within a session of the print - and with Titan, ONGC and M&M only reported after Thursday’s close, today’s open is the next verdict window.

5. The exchange gets its verdict: up. BSE Ltd - which reported its 45% profit quarter after Wednesday’s close - surged more than 5% on Thursday, with Motilal Oswal keeping its Buy and raising earnings estimates on the volume recovery, while Bernstein retained its Underperform rating even as it raised its target to Rs 3,180 from Rs 2,820 (Economic Times); PL Capital tweaked FY27 revenue estimates upward and the bank-guarantee norms overhang persists (Business Standard). BSE Ltd trades only on the NSE - exchanges cannot list on themselves - so its prints are NSE prices, flagged as such. Wednesday’s edition said the verdict on the post-results gap would land Thursday; it landed up. Editor’s takeaway: the market is paying for the derivatives recovery story - the long read this week was BSE’s comeback; the valuation debate between the bulls and Bernstein is now the live one.

6. Anthropic opens its books. Anthropic filed its S-1 with the US SEC on 26 October for a proposed initial public offering (the company’s announcement), and on 2 November released an amended prospectus with its third-quarter financials (CNBC; the filing is on the SEC’s EDGAR system). An AI lab’s numbers - revenue, losses, compute commitments - are now public documents rather than leaks; the amended filing shows third-quarter revenue of $17 billion. Separately, a claim that OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy has joined Anthropic’s pretraining team circulated on aggregation sites this week; this paper found no confirmation on his blog or on Anthropic’s newsroom at press time, so it does not carry the claim. Editor’s takeaway: the AI boom’s most private numbers are becoming its most public ones - the Q3 prospectus is now the primary source for what frontier AI actually costs.

Thursday’s tape, on the record. Sensex 79,310.01 (+2,008.61, +2.60%); Nifty 24,536.60 (+576, +2.40%). Financials and autos led; media and chemicals were the rare losers (India Today). FIIs bought a net Rs 14,974.68 crore - the biggest single day in over a year - while DIIs sold a net Rs 10,444.54 crore (Moneycontrol).

S&P 500 7,353 (-4.4%); Dow 51,523 (-1,833 points, -3.4%); Nasdaq 24,315 (-5.5%, correction territory); Russell 2000 also entered a correction (Kiplinger; AP). Nvidia -9.3% (negative year-to-date), Meta -4.0%, Microsoft -3.6%, Alphabet -2.2%, Qualcomm -9.5%. The Magnificent Seven lost roughly $1 trillion in one session (CNBC).

Oil. Brent settled up more than $3 a barrel Thursday; WTI up more than $2 - both reversing part of Wednesday’s 8%-plus crash to the lowest settlements since 31 August; Brent had briefly touched $93 (Reuters; The National).

The EAAA bond, day four: holding the premium. The 10.8% EAAA bond (BSE symbol 108EAAAL27) closed Thursday at 109,619 - flat on the day and holding a 9.6% premium to its Rs 1,00,000 face value since listing (BSE official data, F series). Repro, day two: the week’s other new listing added 0.86% to close at Rs 316.10 (BSE). In the pipeline: Anthropic’s amended S-1 (front page, story 6) is the filing to read - an AI lab’s third-quarter financials, filed and public.

blocks.html: The why. PI Industries (-18.86% to Rs 1,774.30 - a six-year low per Business Standard) collapsed on a 70% profit fall and a near-halving of margins, the company citing El Nino and generic-pricing pressure (CNBC TV18). On the winners’ side, Bajaj Finance (+7.77% to Rs 1,070.20) and ICICI Bank (+5.29% to Rs 1,499.30) carried the index on the record foreign bid; Asian Paints added 4.46% and HDFC Bank 3.25% (all BSE official closes). Ixigo, Uno Minda, Parag Milk and Ashok Leyland each repriced double digits on results-day momentum in a one-way tape.

Dates for the diary. ONGC declared an Rs 8 per share interim dividend alongside its 47% consolidated profit jump. NBCC declared a 25% interim dividend with its 34% profit rise. NTPC’s Rs 3 first interim dividend has its record date today, Friday 6 November (payment from 25 November). HUL’s Rs 19 interim record date falls Thursday 12 November (payment 25 November). Infosys’s Rs 26 interim pays out on 11 November.

The flow ledger behind Thursday’s record. FIIs bought Rs 31,797.86 crore gross and sold Rs 16,823.18 crore for the net Rs 14,974.68 crore; DIIs went the other way, selling a net Rs 10,444.54 crore (Moneycontrol, on exchange data). The context that makes it a story: foreign investors were net sellers through most of 2026, and Thursday’s print beats the previous single-day record - Rs 12,594 crore on 26 June 2025 - by nearly 19%. Domestic funds turning record sellers on the same day is the handoff to watch: when one wall of money replaces another, the index level depends on who blinks first. The scoreboard going into the Diwali weekend: Sensex 79,310, up 2.60%; the record foreign bid; and a 5.5% Nasdaq rout arriving as the weekend’s homework.

Lenskart’s first verdict as a listed company: passed. The eyewear retailer’s first post-listing quarter - profit up 122.1% to Rs 227.08 crore, revenue up 35.7% to Rs 2,845 crore - sent the stock to a 52-week high of 767.40 intraday before it closed at 718.40, up 3.96% (BSE), and pulled target-price raises from Nomura, Jefferies, Elara, HSBC, Motilal Oswal, CLSA and Macquarie - Citi the lone Neutral (Economic Times; Hindu BusinessLine).

Nykaa’s verdict: the multiple still does the talking. Profit more than tripled to about Rs 101 crore and the stock fell 1.44% - “fails to impress street,” per Business Standard. Two recent consumer listings, two opposite reactions to triple-digit profit growth: the market is pricing growth durability, not growth. CaratLane - Titan’s online jewellery bet, acquired in 2016 for Rs 357 crore - sits inside today’s long read, the startup that became a Tata growth engine.

The political bill for the buildout arrived. Thursday’s 5.5% Nasdaq rout was, per Kiplinger, sparked by concern that Democratic leadership in Washington and in states “from Texas to Ohio” will create headwinds for AI data-center construction - the exact risk this paper’s AI desk flagged after Tuesday’s elections, when governors favouring data-center pauses won and exit polls showed most voters opposing new facilities. The market’s Thursday verdict: Nvidia -9.3% and negative for the year, $1 trillion off the megacap complex, the correction in the Nasdaq official. The counter-file: Anthropic’s amended S-1, filed 2 November, puts third-quarter financials for a frontier lab on the public record (CNBC; Anthropic) - the cost side of the AI boom is now auditable. Not carried: the Karpathy-to-Anthropic claim (front page, story 6) - unverified at his blog and Anthropic’s newsroom at press time. The frame for next week: a correction driven by politics needs a political resolution, and Washington’s leadership races are not settled.

A verification note from this desk’s own workflow, offered because it generalizes. This week a claim that a famous AI researcher had changed employers spread across a dozen aggregation sites within 24 hours - each citing the others, none citing him. Checking the two sources that would actually know (his blog; the employer’s newsroom) took under a minute and returned nothing. The tool lesson for anyone building or researching with AI summaries: aggregators multiply claims; only owning sources confirm them. The faster the summary layer gets, the more the one-minute primary-source check is worth. This paper’s rule - verify at the owning source or drop - held again today.

Test the gold before the weekend. Diwali is Sunday, and this is the country’s biggest gold-buying weekend. If you buy or exchange jewellery this weekend, ask the store to test your old pieces on a purity machine before you settle - the machine tells you in three minutes whether the 22-karat you were sold years ago is really 22-karat. Tanishq built its entire business on that test (today’s long read); most organised jewellers now offer it free. If the number comes back low, that is negotiating information, not an insult.

Every Indian trading day, two walls of institutional money are counted. FIIs (foreign institutional investors) are overseas funds buying Indian stocks; DIIs (domestic institutional investors) are local mutual funds and insurers. The exchanges publish their net buy and sell figures after each session, and the split matters because the two groups often trade against each other: foreigners selling into domestic buying was the 2026 pattern until Thursday, when it flipped violently - a record Rs 14,975 crore of foreign buying against a record Rs 10,444 crore of domestic selling. The flows do not say why anyone traded; they say who has the marginal rupee. When the FII number turns persistently positive after a long outflow streak, rallies get a second engine; when it reverses after one day, Thursday was positioning, not conviction. That is what next week tests. 60-second recall, closed book: (1) What do the daily FII and DII figures count? (2) What made Thursday’s flows historic? (3) What do flows not tell you? Answers: the net buying and selling of foreign and domestic institutional investors; record foreign buying against record domestic selling on the same day; why anyone traded - only who holds the marginal rupee.

A correction is a fall of 10% or more from an index’s most recent peak - a label, not a forecast. The Nasdaq composite entered one on Thursday: its close of 24,315 sits more than 10% below its 6 October high of 27,599.79, as did the Russell 2000. The label matters because it changes behaviour: some systematic funds de-risk at the threshold, and “correction” headlines recruit sellers on their own. Beyond 20% from the peak, the label changes to bear market. Thursday’s correction is, so far, one index and one theme - the AI buildout - not the whole market: the Dow, down 3.4%, remains well short of the line.

The desk’s rule, restated after the 27 October change: every published setup stays on the board until it completes (target hit) or fails (stop hit); the five-session lapse is retired. Per-share prices on every line; the Rs 1,500 price cap screens what qualifies as a setup. Ledger: Slow Burn swing research, 24 Oct.

blocks.html: Setup slots 2 to 5 stay empty today - nothing new cleared the verification bar; an empty slot is a result, not a gap. Thursday’s movers were screened against the six standing factors before being left off: PI Industries has a verified catalyst, but an 18.9% collapse is a falling knife, not a setup - the trend factor fails outright; Ixigo, Uno Minda and Ashok Leyland all repriced double digits in one session, which is chasing, not entry; Bajaj Finance (+7.77% to Rs 1,070.20) cleared its own day on the FII bid but the entry fails the risk-reward screen after a near-8% single-day run. The honest reads on the live lines, with per-share prices: HCLTech (Rs 1,432.00) rose 1.92%, now +3.61% against the cost-adjusted fill of Rs 1,382.13; Thursday’s low of Rs 1,426.45 stayed well above the Rs 1,346.90 stop, which has never traded. Kotak Mahindra Bank (Rs 467.45) held above its Rs 437.55 trigger for a ninth session - still a candidate, not a setup. JSW Steel (Rs 1,353.00) extended above the reclaimed zone; the published R:R screen still fails it, which is why it stays a watchlist line. ONGC (Rs 230.10) slipped 1.90% but held inside its Rs 218.50-238.75 coil for a third session above 228 - and reported a 47% consolidated profit jump with an Rs 8 dividend after the close, while crude rebounded $3 overnight; the coil decides. Infosys (Rs 1,166.10) rallied 3.46% - above the 1,120 floor that keeps the absorption thesis alive, still below the 1,175 trigger zone. Tech Mahindra stays shelved above the Rs 1,500 cap.

blocks.html: Three conditions, in the order they resolve. First, the collision: Thursday gave India its biggest foreign buying day in over a year and then gave New York its worst session since April - Monday’s open prices both, and whether the Rs 14,975 crore was conviction or positioning shows in whether those buyers return after a 5.5% Nasdaq rout. Second, oil’s tripwires: a mined and burning tanker east of Hormuz one day after an 8% crash - whether the seven-conditions reply chain and Araghchi’s calls with Riyadh and Doha outrun the next incident. Third, the AI buildout’s political licence: a correction sparked by election math does not resolve on its own - the tells are the incoming Congress’s first statements on data-center policy and whether the hyperscalers’ capex guidance changes when they next speak. This desk does not predict the answers; it watches these conditions.

The new Congress. Cause chain: Democrats took both chambers on Tuesday (AP), flipping seven Senate seats with a path to 54 (DSCC via NPR); Mississippi and Alaska remain uncalled at press; Trump has offered both an olive branch and a veto hat. Watch next: the final Senate margin, the leadership races, and the first statements on data-center and Iran policy - both now market-moving after Thursday. Proven wrong if: the uncalled races pull the Senate count back to Republican control.

The Hormuz reply chain. Cause chain: Iran’s seven conditions for reopening the strait; a US reply Tehran calls “not convincing”; Qatar shuttling proposals; four tankers caught fire after hitting mines, per the IRGC; two vessels detained - and on Thursday, Iran’s navy said another tanker struck a mine and caught fire east of the strait, while Araghchi called his Saudi and Qatari counterparts. Oil crashed 8% Wednesday and settled up $3-plus Thursday. Watch next: UKMTO confirmations on further incidents, Tehran’s counter-reply, and whether the detained tankers are released. Proven wrong if: a signed reopening of the strait lands while tankers are still being detained.

The FII reversal. Cause chain: foreign investors sold Indian equities through most of 2026; on Thursday they bought a record net Rs 14,975 crore while domestic funds sold a record Rs 10,444 crore; hours later, Wall Street’s AI complex lost $1 trillion. Watch next: the provisional flow prints on Friday and Monday - whether the foreign bid survives the US rout, and whether domestic selling persists into the Diwali week. Proven wrong if: Friday’s flows show the foreign bid was a one-day positioning event ahead of the weekend.

edition.title: The foreigners' Rs 15,000 crore day, and Wall Street's AI hangover
edition.fact: Edition 32. The foreigners' Rs 15,000 crore day, and Wall Street's AI hangover. Friday 6 November 2026, edition 32. This edition runs 4,567 words. Foreign investors bought Rs 14,975 crore of Indian stocks on Thursday - the biggest single-day foreign purchase in over a year - and the Sensex jumped 2,009 points on the eve of the Diwali weekend. Hours later, Wall Street's AI trade broke: the Nasdaq fell 5.5% into correction, its worst day since April 2025, on fears that America's new Democratic leadership will slow the data-center buildout. Oil reversed: Brent settled up more than $3 after another tanker attack east of Hormuz. And the results flood delivered its verdicts: Titan's profit more than doubled, PI Industries' collapsed 70%, and the Lenskart and Nykaa gaps resolved in opposite directions. The long read is Titan - the watch company that almost died selling jewellery, saved by a machine that exposed the whole industry's lie.
edition.intro: The 5-minute lead route is first; sections carry the detail. The long read: how a Tata watch venture wandered into jewellery, nearly sank on 18-karat Western designs, and built Tanishq on a purity machine - pegged to Thursday's quarter, where profit more than doubled.
